stem.text: The function \( h \) is twice differentiable for all real \( x \). Selected values of \( h \) and of its derivative \( h' \) are given in the table. \[ \begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & 0 & 2 & 3 & 5 & 8 \\ \hline h(x) & 4 & -2 & 1 & 7 & 1 \\ h'(x) & -5 & -1 & 3 & 2 & -4 \end{array} \]

parts.prompt: Find the average rate of change of \( h \) over the interval \( 0 \le x \le 8 \). Show the computation that leads to your answer.

worked_solution.text: Difference of the endpoint values of h divided by the length of the interval.

points.criterion: Writes (h(8) - h(0))/(8 - 0) with the table values, (1 - 4)/8, and gives -3/8. The unsimplified quotient (1 - 4)/8 and the decimal -0.375 are accepted.

parts.prompt: Must there be a value \( c \), with \( 0 < c < 2 \), at which \( h'(c) = -3 \)? Must there be a value \( r \), with \( 3 < r < 5 \), at which \( h'(r) = 3 \)? Justify each answer.

worked_solution.text: Average rate of change of h over 0 to 2.
h is differentiable, so it is continuous on the closed interval and differentiable on the open one; the Mean Value Theorem gives c.
Average rate of change of h over 3 to 5.
The same hypotheses hold on this interval, so the Mean Value Theorem gives r.

points.criterion: Shows the average rate of change of h over 0 <= x <= 2 as a difference quotient with values, (-2 - 4)/(2 - 0), equal to -3. The bare value -3 with no quotient shown does not earn the point.

Answers yes for c, stating that h is differentiable (so continuous on 0 <= x <= 2 and differentiable on 0 < x < 2) and that the Mean Value Theorem therefore guarantees c with h'(c) = -3. An appeal to the Intermediate Value Theorem does not earn the point.

Shows the average rate of change of h over 3 <= x <= 5 as a difference quotient with values, (7 - 1)/(5 - 3), equal to 3. Citing h'(3) = 3 from the table instead does not earn the point, since x = 3 is not in the open interval.

Answers yes for r, stating continuity of h on 3 <= x <= 5 and differentiability on 3 < x < 5 (or that h is differentiable) and invoking the Mean Value Theorem. Reporting r = 3 from the table does not earn the point.

parts.prompt: Must there be a value \( w \), with \( 3 < w < 8 \), at which \( h'(w) = 0 \)? Justify your answer.

worked_solution.text: The endpoint values are equal, so the average rate of change is zero.
h is continuous on the closed interval and differentiable on the open one, so the Mean Value Theorem (or Rolle's Theorem) gives w.

points.criterion: Shows (h(8) - h(3))/(8 - 3) = (1 - 1)/5 = 0, or states h(3) = h(8) = 1 as the equal endpoint values.
Answers yes, stating continuity on 3 <= x <= 8 and differentiability on 3 < x < 8 (or that h is differentiable) and invoking the Mean Value Theorem or Rolle's Theorem.

parts.prompt: Must there be a value \( v \), with \( 2 < v < 5 \), at which \( h''(v) = 1 \)? Justify your answer.

worked_solution.text: Apply the average rate of change to h' this time.
h is twice differentiable, so h' is differentiable and hence continuous on the closed interval; the Mean Value Theorem applied to h' gives v.

points.criterion: Shows the average rate of change of h' over 2 <= x <= 5, (h'(5) - h'(2))/(5 - 2) = (2 - (-1))/3, equal to 1. A quotient built from values of h instead of h' does not earn the point.
Answers yes, stating that h' is differentiable (because h is twice differentiable), hence continuous on 2 <= x <= 5 and differentiable on 2 < x < 5, and applying the Mean Value Theorem to h'.
